title: Indian Chefs Put Bone Marrow Centre Stage, Sanghvi Notes in Rude Food
excerpt: Once hidden inside nihari and paya, roasted bone marrow is now a headline dish in Mumbai and Delhi — from Paradox's thecha marrow to The Bombay Canteen's kachori and Plats' steak crusts.
body:
• Vir Sanghvi's Rude Food column in Hindustan Times Brunch argues Indian chefs are finally putting bone marrow at the centre of the menu, not just inside nihari and paya.
  • At Paradox in Mumbai, Varun Totlani serves roasted marrow with thecha, caramelised onions, basil and kaffir lime, scooped with purple potato chips.
  • The Bombay Canteen tucks marrow into a short rib kachori, Veronica's folds it into burger grinds, O Pedro serves it in tamarind gravy, and Plats in Delhi uses bone fat for steak crusts.
  • Chefs link the shift to diners who have eaten marrow abroad, want the same at home, and value nose-to-tail cooking that uses the whole animal.

Bone marrow spent generations inside Indian gravies. It melted into nalli nihari, enriched paya, and disappeared into slow broths before most diners noticed it was there. In his Rude Food column for Hindustan Times Brunch, Vir Sanghvi makes a different point: Indian chefs are finally serving marrow on its own, roasted in the bone and placed in front of the diner as the dish itself.

The change is visible across menus that have been documented in detail elsewhere. Esquire India described marrow moving from a background note in nihari and paya to toast-toppers, burgers and tasting-menu courses, with chefs treating a once-humble offcut as a headline ingredient.

Mumbai puts marrow in the centre

At Paradox in Mumbai, head chef Varun Totlani, who also leads Masque, serves roasted marrow with thecha, caramelised onions, basil, pickled onion and kaffir lime, scooped up with purple potato chips. Diners can then pour a shot through the emptied bone, a piece of theatre Totlani told Esquire India he would like to see become a ritual at the restaurant.

Totlani linked the demand to travel. "Diners have become far more open to trying bold textures and flavours," he said. "They've experienced global menus while travelling, and they want to have similar experiences back home, too."

Hussain Shahzad, executive chef at Hunger Inc. Hospitality, puts marrow in several forms across his Mumbai restaurants. At The Bombay Canteen it is tucked into a beef short rib and bone marrow kachori with smoked onion curry and tadka dahi. At Veronica's it is folded into burger grinds with dry-aged short ribs for a smash patty. At O Pedro it arrives in tamarind gravy with pickles and Goan poee.

"Bone marrow has always been part of our food culture. And now, it's not intimidating or over the top — it is actually pretty fun and approachable."

— Hussain Shahzad, executive chef, Hunger Inc. Hospitality

Delhi and the diaspora table

In Delhi, Plats chef and co-founder Jamsheed Bhot swaps butter for bone fat to build flavour and moisture into steak crusts, calling marrow rich, fatty and full of umami. He also pointed to collagen as part of the appeal for health-aware diners, according to Esquire India.

The same logic is travelling with Indian restaurants abroad. Bombay Brasserie's new menu in Singapore, reviewed this month, includes a Bone Marrow Masala Toast: marrow roasted for 12 to 17 minutes at 230 degrees Celsius, seasoned with nihari-inspired spices and spread on bread with nihari butter. Executive chef Areeb Rehman's version keeps the European roasted-marrow format but flavours it from Uttar Pradesh, where nihari is central, as reported in the Bombay Brasserie menu review.

Why now

Three reasons recur in the chefs' own explanations. First, exposure: Indian diners who have eaten roasted marrow in London, New York or Singapore ask for it at home. Second, sustainability: using marrow is nose-to-tail cooking, a way to value the whole animal rather than only prime cuts — a point all three chefs in the Esquire India report emphasised. Third, technique: marrow rewards precision. Roast it too long and it melts away; undercook it and it clings to the bone. Shahzad soaks bones in salted iced water for hours to draw out blood and clean the flavour, and prefers hind femur for its fat-to-bone ratio.

For diaspora readers, the dish to look for on a menu is the simplest test of the trend: roasted marrow served in the bone, with something sharp or hot alongside — thecha, pickled onion, or nihari spice — and bread, chips or paratha to scoop it. If a restaurant near you lists it as a starter rather than hiding it in a curry, Sanghvi's point has reached your city too.
